newsitem.title: CONGO: Fresh Congo firing, evacuations, France to leave.
newsitem.headline: Fresh Congo firing, evacuations, France to leave.

text.p: France evacuated more civilians from the Congo Republic's capital on Sunday after fresh shooting around the international airport, and prepared to start pulling its troops out of the battered city.

Envoys of President Pascal Lissouba and his predecessor, former Marxist military leader Denis Sassou Nguesso, took advantage of the same lull in firing at the airport and left for peace talks in Gabon. They travelled on the same plane.

"We start pulling out in principle on Monday and that will take something less than a week," French army spokesman Henry Pelissier told Reuters as about 100 men, women and children waited to leave on final flights out.
An earlier French plane left with dozens of civilians, mostly Africans, for the Congolese port of Pointe Noire.

The conflict started on June 5 after the army surrounded Sassou Nguesso's home as part of a crackdown on private militias and unauthorised arms in the runup to a July 27 election in the oil-producing former French colony in Central Africa.
Militia loyal to Sassou Nguesso advanced on the airport on Sunday and bombarded troops loyal to Lissouba there with shells and mortar bombs from 2 a.m. til the middle of the day.
The barrage followed two days of relative calm in the city and diplomatic efforts to end over a week of ethnic and political killing. The two sides declared a truce on Wednesday.
Lissouba, interviewed by Radio France International on Sunday, called for the election to take place as planned and repeated a call for an African peace force to oversee polling.
"These elections must take place," he said. "Democracy cannot be negotiated."
Sassou Nguesso did not rule out the idea. "The international community must organise the elections, check them and ensure security," he told the same radio station.
Mediators say Gabon's veteran President Omar Bongo will host peace talks on Monday in his capital Libreville.

French Ambassador Raymond Cesaire, who announced the departure of the envoys, played down Sunday's fighting. "These things happen during negotiations when sides try to improve their positions," he said.
Envoys representing Lissouba and Sassou Nguesso agreed on Saturday to meet in Gabon on implementing a peace deal.

Brazzaville mayor and mediator Bernard Kolelas, whose supporters were in the thick of bloody clashes that killed 2,000 people after a disputed parliamentary election in 1993, has been at the heart of the negotiations. His militia has stayed out of the fighting this time.
U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun and the U.S. and French ambassadors to Brazzaville have also been closely involved.

Bodies litter Brazzaville's streets and the smell of rotting bodies permeates parts of the city. Some sources say the death toll could run into hundreds and maybe even several thousand but many of the dead lay uncollected where they fell.
"The number of bodies in the morgue is uncountable," surgeon Kibongo Nazerne said at the main University Hospital Centre. "It has space for 140 bodies but there are many more than that."
France has evacuated almost 5,000 foreign nationals, about a third of them French. It planned to end the airlifts on Sunday.
Kolelas aides and Lissouba have floated the idea of French troops staying. Sassou Nguesso is cooler on the idea. Both Lissouba and Sassou Nguesso say they want the poll to go ahead.
Pope John Paul, addressing pilgrims at the Vatican on Sunday, condemned the fighting and urged reconciliation.
